newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian security chief meets Chechen rebels.
newsitem.headline: New Russian security chief meets Chechen rebels.

text.p: Russia's new security chief Ivan Rybkin met Chechen rebel leaders on Sunday for the first time, declaring he wanted to continue peace efforts begun by his ousted predecessor Alexander Lebed.

"We will talk about the mechanism of a return to peaceful life and what is needed to make economic revival work and ensure people's normal activities," Rybkin told reporters on arrival in Ingushetia, the region neighbouring war-torn Chechnya.
"We will discuss everything in detail and with no haste."

Rybkin later held a closed meeting with former rebel military commander Aslan Mashkadov and two other separatist officials in the Ingush president's residence near the regional capital Nazran, Itar-Tass news agency said.

The separatists have said they are worried that Lebed's dismissal this month could jeopardise the peace deal he signed with them in late August, ending 21 months of fighting in the tiny North Caucasus region.
Rybkin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin have been at pains to reassure them that Moscow does not want a return to the violence which killed tens of thousands of people.
But a lasting peace is still a long way off and disagreements continue over control of the breakaway region, which Moscow insists must remain in the Russian Federation.

Earlier Rybkin, who had been expected to head straight for Chechnya, spent the day in Ingushetia, visiting a school, printing house and hotel built on the proceeds of a special economic zone set up there, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Meanwhile the rebel leaders attended a congress in southwestern Chechnya at which they said there could be no compromise on independence from Moscow.

Conservative Kremlin officials and members of parliament cite such provocative comments to explain their opposition to the August 31 peace deal, which the rebels have treated as a victory in their battle to split Chechnya from Moscow.
The agreement called for the withdrawal of Russian troops and said discussions on Chechnya's future status should be put on hold for five years.

But the rebels later confirmed their plans to seek independence, took Chechnya under their control and unilaterally formed a "coalition government", defying an earlier agreement to cooperate with Russia in creating a post-war authority.

"Chechen independence cannot be subject to trade-offs and compromises," rebel spokesman Ruslan Martagov quoted separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev as telling Sunday's Congress of the Chechen People, Interfax news agency reported.
"After the defeat of the million-strong Russian army, the Chechen people have a right to dictate their conditions to Moscow," Martagov quoted another leader as saying.
Some 1,500 delegates approved plans to hold local elections in January and put forward Yandarbiyev as a candidate for president, Tass said.
Yandarbiyev became rebel leader in April after his predecessor Dzhokhar Dudayev, who declared Chechnya independent in 1991, was reported killed in a Russian rocket attack.

The Chechen congress opened in a Grozny building but delegates then moved to Urus-Martan, 35 km (20 miles) southwest of the capital, following a telephoned bomb warning, Tass said. An initial police search found no trace of a device.
Separatist leaders said on Saturday they opposed Moscow's plans to keep two brigades permanently in Chechnya, insisting all troops should leave.
